content: The analysis revealed that certain dietary patterns created nutrient gaps, particularly when fortified foods or specific food groups were excluded. For example, patterns with daily micronutrient powders (MNPs) lacked whole grains and legumes, which are rich in magnesium. Further refinement of these patterns could address such gaps while still meeting nutrient targets. Including small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) daily reduced, but did not eliminate, the iron gap (59% of the nutrient reference value [NRV] compared to 28% in the best-case scenario). However, this approach also introduced gaps for magnesium, potassium (76% of NRV), and choline (82% of NRV), while exceeding the upper limit (UL) for zinc. Additional iterations would be necessary to balance these excesses and deficiencies, though achieving this may be challenging without eliminating staple foods entirely, as SQ-LNS displaced other complementary foods. Daily servings of Super Cereal Plus increased the iron gap and created new gaps for several minerals, thiamin, and choline, as it displaced other nutrient-rich foods. Models incorporating fortified items suggested that lower-cost, lower-quality food patterns could meet nutrient needs if fortified items were included. For instance, daily MNPs resulted in a food pattern with minimal starchy staples, very small amounts of egg (less than one per week), diverse vegetables, and a daily serving of 60g (one-quarter cup) of milk. Most nutrient needs could be met without flesh foods, but not without vegetables and dairy. Iterative adjustments could address low magnesium levels. For SQ-LNS and Super Cereal Plus, food patterns were monotonous due to the displacement of other foods. These patterns primarily consisted of breast milk, the fortified item, and minimal staple foods. They failed to meet all target nutrient needs and would likely require reducing breast milk intake to allow for more complementary foods. For infants aged 9 months, modifying food patterns by eliminating food groups, restricting staples to one type, or increasing staple quantities had little impact on nutrient gaps. However, iron gaps increased slightly in many scenarios, and a small fat gap emerged when staple foods were increased to 21 servings per week. Except for iron and vitamin D, many food patterns could meet nutrient needs for this age group if a diversity of whole grains, fruits, vegetables, and protein foods were included. Adding one unhealthy item per day did not create nutrient gaps, though scenarios with multiple unhealthy items were not modeled. For younger infants, fortified items eliminated carbohydrate gaps and significantly reduced vitamin D gaps, though vitamin D levels remained at only 43-54% of the NRV with daily fortified item consumption. Super Cereal Plus did not reduce the iron gap, while MNPs three days per week or SQ-LNS seven days per week improved iron levels to 80-85% of NRVs. Daily MNPs eliminated the iron gap entirely. Scenarios with daily SQ-LNS did not introduce new gaps for target nutrients but exceeded the UL for zinc. Food patterns with MNPs or SQ-LNS seven days per week reduced staple foods to the minimum allowed, increased fruits, decreased vegetable variety, and eliminated or nearly eliminated protein foods. Dairy was increased with MNPs but eliminated with daily SQ-LNS, reflecting differences in calcium content between the two items. For infants aged 9 months, target nutrient needs could be met without fortified products, though scenarios with fortified products were less diverse. These patterns included fewer servings of whole grains and flesh foods and, except for MNPs, fewer servings of dairy. However, they still included three to five types of fruits and vegetables daily. Sensitivity analyses excluding flesh foods and assuming 5% iron absorption showed that daily MNPs eliminated the iron gap, while SQ-LNS reduced but did not eliminate it. Super Cereal Plus had a smaller impact on reducing the iron gap. For older infants (9 months and above), feasible best-case patterns had no gaps for target nutrients. However, eliminating food groups introduced new gaps. For example, scenarios without vegetables or animal-source protein foods introduced iron gaps (88-94% of NRV). Scenarios without animal-source protein foods also introduced a small gap for vitamin B12 (95% of NRV), while those without fruits or vegetables introduced a small fiber gap (96% of NRV). Restricting starchy staples to one type or increasing their quantity did not introduce new gaps, provided a diversity of fruits, vegetables, and protein foods was included. Including one unhealthy item up to seven days per week did not create new gaps, though multiple unhealthy items were not modeled. Many modified scenarios slightly exceeded the UL for copper. Real-world food patterns, approximated using data from rural Bangladesh, rural southern Malawi, and Mexico, showed substantial differences from modeled best-case scenarios. Nutrient content in these patterns often fell short of target values for most nutrients, except for protein, fatty acids, vitamins A and C, and niacin. In Bangladesh and Malawi, gaps for choline, B vitamins, and minerals were common across all age groups. Mexico had fewer gaps, particularly for older children, but gaps for several B vitamins and minerals remained. Carbohydrate and vitamin D levels were consistently low across all settings. Fortified items partially addressed these gaps, with MNPs and SQ-LNS having the most positive impacts. However, nutrient gaps persisted in all three settings. The study highlighted strengths, such as the use of data from 37 countries and the development of comprehensive food subgroup nutrient profiles. However, limitations included the lack of globally representative data, challenges with food composition data, and the inability to model all desirable scenarios. The results should be interpreted cautiously, as they provide general insights rather than specific food-based recommendations.
